summary: Two satirical trials in one chapter. First Bel: the king's god that 'eats' seventy measures of food a day — Daniel scatters ashes on the temple floor, and by morning the footprints of 'men, women, and children' lead to the priests' secret door. Then the dragon: Daniel kills it without sword or staff, with cakes of boiled pitch, fat, and hair. Enraged, Babylon forces the king to throw Daniel to seven lions — where the prophet Habakkuk is airlifted by an angel, dinner in hand, for six days. On the seventh, the king finds Daniel alive and confesses: 'Great art thou, O Lord the God of Daniel.'
whyItMatters: This is Scripture at its most comic — and the comedy is theology. Every idol fails the same empirical test: what you worship should not leave footprints. The chapter argues against idolatry not with thunder but with evidence, and ends with a pagan king's confession of the living God.

context.author: Unknown; Greek addition to Daniel, in circulation by the 2nd-1st century BC
context.date: Set in the reign of Cyrus of Persia; composed in the Greek period
context.setting: Babylon — the temple of Bel, the dragon's pit, and the lions' den

outline.heading: Bel's appetite
outline.note: The king worships what the food budget feeds; Daniel smiles

outline.heading: The wager and the ashes
outline.note: Sealed temple, footprints in the ash, the priests exposed

outline.heading: The dragon slain

outline.heading: Daniel in the den

keyVerses.text: Then Daniel smiled and said: O king, be not deceived: for this is but clay within, and brass without, neither hath he eaten at any time.
keyVerses.why: The chapter's thesis in one smile — worship what is living, not what is plated.

keyVerses.text: And the king said: I see the footsteps of men, and women, and children. And the king was angry.
keyVerses.why: Forensic evidence in the Bible: the idol's divinity dies on the pavement it walked on.

keyVerses.text: Then Daniel took pitch, and fat, and hair, and boiled them together: and he made lumps, and put them into the dragon's mouth, and the dragon burst asunder. And he said: Behold him whom you worshipped.
keyVerses.why: The dragon dies of dinner — the satire's sharpest point: the 'living god' is killed by the same stuff that kills any animal.

keyVerses.text: And Daniel said: Thou hast remembered me, O God, and thou hast not forsaken them that love thee.
keyVerses.why: Daniel's thanksgiving over the prophet's dinner — provision in a lions' den, six days in.

questions.question: Why isn't this chapter in Protestant Bibles?
questions.answer: Like Susanna (chapter 13), it belongs to the Greek additions to Daniel — the Hebrew/Aramaic Daniel has twelve chapters. The Vulgate numbered it Daniel 14, and Catholic and Orthodox Bibles retain it there; Protestant Bibles follow the shorter Hebrew canon. It survives in two Greek forms, which is why the opening differs slightly between the Septuagint (Astyages) and the version behind this chapter (Cyrus).

questions.question: Is the story meant to be funny?
questions.answer: Yes — deliberately. Daniel 'smiles' at Bel (14:6), 'laughs' at the footprints scene (1:19 in the standalone Septuagint book), and the dragon 'bursts asunder' from indigestion. The comedy is polemic: laughter is a weapon against idolatry, the same strategy Elijah uses on Carmel when he suggests Baal might be asleep.

questions.question: Who is Habakkuk doing in a lions' den story?
questions.answer: The prophet Habakkuk, 'in Judea,' is carried by the hair of his head to Babylon with a bowl of pottage for Daniel — a legendary transport that ties the tale to a recognized prophetic name. The episode gave art history one of its strangest images (Rubens painted it) and makes the point that God feeds his servants through surprising couriers.

questions.question: Why does the king convert at the end?
questions.answer: Because the evidence overwhelmed him: the idol debunked, the dragon dead, Daniel alive after six days among seven starved lions. His confession — 'he is the Saviour, working signs and wonders in the earth' (14:42) — is the chapter's goal: not Daniel's survival, but the pagan throne acknowledging the living God.

questions.question: Does this contradict Daniel 6, the famous lions' den story?
questions.answer: They are separate tales with different kings (Darius in Daniel 6, Cyrus here), different conspiracies, and different outcomes for the accusers. The Greek additions freely reuse the den motif — a sign they are popular stories about the same hero, not competing reports of one event.

glossary.def: 'Lord' — the Babylonian god Marduk, whose temple cultus the story satirizes.
Tar — boiled with fat and hair into dense, indigestible lumps.
The prophet of the book of Habakkuk, brought by an angel from Judea.
The Median king named in the Septuagint's opening; this chapter begins with Cyrus.
